title: #61 Sometimes Mini-Whiteboards Are Not the Best Way to Collect Whole-Class Data
author: Barton, Craig
summary: A self-professed mini-whiteboard enthusiast, Barton nonetheless argues the tool isn't ideal for every kind of question, specifically ones with a small, finite set of possible answers. He walks through three classroom examples where mini-whiteboards made data collection unreliable: a multiple-choice diagnostic question where it was hard to see which option each student had chosen at a glance; a comparison question where 30 students' boards produced too much data to process at once; and a true/false-style exercise made worse by dirty boards and small handwriting. For each, he proposes narrower, faster alternatives -- coloured ABCD cards for multiple choice, a sequential show-of-hands for comparisons, and thumbs up/down for correct/incorrect judgments -- arguing these reduce the flow of data a teacher must process in the few seconds available. His conclusion is that whiteboards remain useful for showing working, but a second, more targeted checking tool should be layered on top when the goal is a fast, accurate read of whole-class understanding.
points: Mini-whiteboards excel at open-ended written responses but become unreliable exactly where the answer set is small, because 30 simultaneous boards produce more visual data than a teacher can parse in a few seconds.
For multiple-choice diagnostic questions, coloured ABCD cards give a faster, more legible read than scanning handwritten letters across 30 boards.
For binary or narrow comparisons, a sequential hands-up check reduces the data stream to one option at a time instead of asking for everything simultaneously.
Barton's broader point is a design principle, not a rejection of whiteboards: match the data-collection tool to the shape of the answer space rather than defaulting to one tool for every check.
quotes: I know of no more efficient way to ascertain the effort and understanding of all students than to ask them to write their answer to a question on a mini-whiteboard and show me on cue.
Notice how difficult it is to identify students’ choices of answers, especially those at the back.
My preferred way of collecting data for multiple-choice diagnosis questions is to use coloured ABCD cards or head down first on head.
With 30 students in the class, there was too much data to identify who was correct and who was not.
This was difficult to see, compounded by dirty boards and small writing.

In each of the examples above, whiteboards could be used for students to do their working out on, but then another tool could have been used to make the required quick-fire analysis of the data more manageable.
